scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Secret Dance of the Druid Bird
This is Drui. Ancient / Medieval to present.
on_screen: Title card: Drui · Ireland · Ancient / Medieval to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The origins of the midwinter wren hunt and its associated dances lie in ancient Celtic paganism and winter solstice rituals.
The Old Irish word for wren, drean, derives from druí-én, meaning 'druid bird', reflecting its historical association with prophecy and augury.
In medieval Irish lore, such as the Life of Saint Moling, the wren is described as the 'magus bird'.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Celebrated annually on 26 December (Saint Stephen's Day or Boxing Day, known as Lá an Dreoilín), the event historically ensured prosperity and good luck for households in the coming year.
Feathers from the wren were distributed to donors as protective amulets against witchcraft and supernatural harm.
The evening gathered funds and food to host a 'wren dance' or 'wren's wake', which functioned as a vital seasonal social event bringing unmarried young people together.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance takes place in two primary settings: as an informal processing movement from door to door, and as a structured ring dance (ringelreihen) around a central pole or sacred space.
On the Isle of Man, after a sacrificed wren was given funeral rites, a living wren was placed inside a wicker cage within a decorated 'wren bush' on a pole.
The community performed a circular ring dance around the pole.
Watch for Wren Pole Circling.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Linear processional outdoor street path ending in a circular ring dance around a central pole.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is driven by lively folk music performed by travelling bands of Wrenboys or Céilí groups.
Traditional instruments include bodhráns (drums), fifes, melodeons, and tin whistles.
Listen for the Bodhrán, Fife, Melodeon, Tin whistle.
The pulse is 2/4, 4/4 or 6/8 at about 120 beats a minute.
Bright acoustic folk sound dominated by rhythmic frame-drum beat, lively melodeon chords, high-pitched fife or whistle tunes, and spirited group singing.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Participants traditionally wear intricate disguises to obscure their identities.

Common costumes feature conical hats and suits made of woven straw (Strawboys), masks fashioned from goat, rabbit, or horse skin, or suits of motley clothing trimmed with greenery, holly, ivy, and ribbons.
In Kerry, processions are accompanied by a hobby horse called the Láir Bhán.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Folklorist Mona Douglas recorded detailed Manx accounts of the wren pole dance and release ritual.

Traditional performers like sean-nós singer Seosamh Ó hÉanaí preserved oral lore and songs surrounding the tradition, while modern folk groups like Steeleye Span, Lankum, and The Chieftains have recorded wren tunes.

While central to Irish and Manx folklore, parallel midwinter traditions existed across Wales (Hela'r Dryw), England (such as Boxing Day dances in Suffolk), France (Fête du Roi de l'Oiseau in Puy-en-Velay and Carcassonne), and Galicia (Caceria do rei Charlo).
Rooted in pre-Christian Celtic solstice celebrations and animal sacrifice rituals.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Historically associated with Celtic pagan solstice sacrifice and augury rituals. Modern revivals are secular or charitable, but historical practice involved sacred bird sacrifice and ritual burial.

scenes.title: Until next time
narration: On St. Stephen's Day, masked dancers in straw and greenery take to the streets to revive an ancient Celtic solstice ritual.
